analysis.one_liner: Limits the biggest meatpackers' market share and bars them from retail stores and livestock futures trading.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors and an unfavorable review from the Small Business Administration, never reaching a House vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have restricted the largest meatpacking companies to no more than 25% of the national slaughter of cattle and hogs, barred them from owning retail meat stores, and banned price discrimination and below-cost selling aimed at pushing small packers out of business. It also would have prohibited big packers and their officers from trading livestock futures, except for legitimate hedging, and let small packers sue violators for triple damages. Enforcement would have run through the Small Business Administration.
analysis.who_benefits: Small and independent meatpacking firms, ranchers and hog farmers who would face more competing buyers for their livestock, and consumers whose grocery meat prices depend on how much competition exists between the few giant packers that dominate slaughter. The bill also let small packers injured by violations recover triple damages plus attorney's fees in federal court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small meatpackers, livestock farmers, and shoppers

how_it_helps.text: Caps any single packer at 25% of the national slaughter for steers and heifers, cows and bulls, or hogs, directly breaking up the concentration in meat processing that the bill's findings say burdens small business.
Prohibits large packers from owning or operating any retail meat outlet, stopping meat companies from using control of both processing and retail to squeeze independent grocers and small packers.
Bans price discrimination between different purchasers in a marketing area and below-cost selling intended to impair small packers, giving independent firms protection against predatory pricing.

Prohibits packers required to report under the Packers and Stockyards Act from trading livestock futures (beyond bona fide hedges) and bars their officers from futures transactions, targeting market manipulation and speculation in the cattle and hog markets.

Lets any small meatpacking concern (under a 5% national slaughter share) injured by a violation sue in district court for treble damages plus attorney's fees, and fines knowing violations up to $500,000 per offense, with each day a continuing violation counted separately.

analysis.who_pays: The handful of very large meatpacking companies, which would have had to shed retail outlets and shrink or split operations to fit under the 25% slaughter cap, pay fines up to $500,000 per offense, and exit livestock futures trading. To the extent the giants lost scale economies, some of the cost could have shown up in meat prices.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement was indirect: the SBA could only file a complaint that another federal department or agency then had to investigate and decide whether to act, a chain that critics could call too slow and too weak to police giant packers.

The flat 25% cap applied regardless of efficiency or investment, and the futures ban reached even personal transactions by officers of any packer reporting under the Packers and Stockyards Act, rules that a supporter would have to admit are blunt instruments.
The Small Business Administration returned an unfavorable executive comment on the bill, the only formal agency reaction on record.

By forcing the largest packers to divest retail outlets and cut slaughter volume, the bill risked some loss of economies of scale, which could raise processing costs and, eventually, retail meat prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real and growing problem, concentration of cattle and hog slaughter in a few giant firms, with remedies (a market-share cap, a retail-ownership ban, anti-predatory-pricing rules, and private treble-damages suits) that would have given small packers and livestock sellers real leverage. But it was bluntly designed: the cap was rigid, the enforcement path through the SBA was convoluted, the officer-level futures ban was overbroad, and the government's only on-record reaction, from the SBA, was unfavorable. A better-crafted version might have achieved the same pro-competition goals with fewer side effects; as written, the costs fell almost entirely on the big packers, which was the point.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Agriculture and Small Business Committees and their subcommittees for two years and died when the Congress ended, without a single hearing vote, markup, or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Neal Smith of Iowa introduced the bill on January 3, 1991, opening day of the 102nd Congress, and it was referred jointly to the Agriculture and Small Business Committees.
No one joined him: the bill finished with zero cosponsors.

The Agriculture Committee sent it to its Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Subcommittee and the Small Business Committee to its SBA and Minority Enterprise subcommittees, where the bill's limits on big packers would have been considered; neither committee ever reported it out.
The Agriculture Committee requested comments from USDA and the SBA; USDA never responded on the record, and on April 5, 1991, the SBA returned an unfavorable executive comment.
No further action was ever taken, and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest meatpacking companies, which kept their market shares, retail ventures, and freedom to trade livestock futures; nothing in the record shows any countervailing gain to small packers, ranchers, or consumers.

for.name: Rep. Neal Edward Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 102nd Congress and pursued no cosponsors who signed on

against.name: House Agriculture Committee and House Small Business Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee and subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress without a markup or a vote, never reporting it to the floor

against.name: Small Business Administration
against.what_they_did: Returned an unfavorable executive comment on the bill

against.name: US Department of Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Was asked for an executive comment in January 1991 and never provided one on the record

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape was never tested beyond its single Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The 25% slaughter cap, ban on owning retail meat outlets, and anti-predatory-pricing rules would have forced the giants to shrink or divest and exposed them to $500,000-per-offense fines and treble-damages suits by small rivals. Their dominance over cattle and hog prices and retail meat supply is exactly what the bill targeted.

Packers required to report under the Packers and Stockyards Act would have been barred from livestock futures other than bona fide hedges, and their officers banned from futures transactions entirely, cutting a class of large traders out of the cattle and hog futures markets.
Firms under a 5% national slaughter share would have gained legal protection from price discrimination and below-cost selling, plus a private right to sue for treble damages and attorney's fees.
Independent grocers and butchers would have been shielded from packer-owned retail outlets, while any grocery chains affiliated with large packers would have had to divest meat retail operations.
